clue.text: Bowman who aims for heart of target

definitions.text: Bowman who aims for heart of target

parts.words: Bowman who aims for heart of target
parts.note: the archer here is the winged god of love, whose arrows are aimed at lovers' hearts rather than a bullseye

explanation.surface: An archer concentrates on the bullseye at the centre of the target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart of target' looks like the bullseye; it is a literal heart, the target of the love god's arrows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of love is pictured as a winged boy with a bow, shooting arrows into people's hearts.

clue.text: A bowler obviously suits him when he's driving

definitions.text: A bowler obviously suits him when he's driving

parts.words: A bowler obviously suits him when he's driving
parts.note: a bowler sounds like a hat worn by a motorist, but here it is a player who delivers the ball and drives means hitting it hard

explanation.surface: A man in a bowler hat looks just right at the wheel of his car.
explanation.walkthrough: A bowler is a hat and driving is motoring on the surface; in the game played with bat and ball, bowlers bowl and batsmen drive.
explanation.definitionFit: A player of the English bat-and-ball game may be a bowler, and a drive is a forceful batting stroke.

clue.text: Clear one in the plot

indicators.note: the letter for one goes inside the word for the plot

parts.note: a plan is a plot or scheme
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A single obvious feature in a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' is a scheme, PLAN, not a storyline.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obvious and easy to understand is evident or simple.

clue.text: Pursue deal for tree

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow or pursue them
deal is fir or pine timber, a wood

explanation.surface: A command to chase a bargain for a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deal' looks like a bargain; it is softwood timber.
explanation.definitionFit: The flowering shrub with hard wood, genus Cornus, is a small tree.

clue.text: One after victory takes the gold

parts.note: a victory is a success
OR is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Someone who follows a winning performance collects the gold medal.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold, a crossword staple; 'takes' simply joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever comes next in a post or line of inheritance follows, or comes after, the previous holder.

clue.text: Nimble creature needed to thwart outside right

indicators.note: the word for thwart is wrapped round the letter for right

parts.note: to spite someone is to thwart or annoy them

explanation.surface: An agile animal is called for to block a winger on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside right' looks like a football position, but 'outside' places SPITE around R.
explanation.definitionFit: An elf or fairy is a small, nimble, mischievous supernatural being.

clue.text: Copper and vanadium liner shaped for old gun

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: the letters are formed into a new shape, rearranged

parts.note: V is the chemical symbol for vanadium
taken as written

explanation.surface: A metal alloy lining is cast to make a cannon.
explanation.walkthrough: CU, V and LINER together are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-barrelled cannon of the 16th and 17th centuries is an early artillery piece.

clue.text: Space in Fleet Street to stay, though it's a squeeze

parts.note: Fleet Street was the home of the London newspaper printing trade, where an em is a space the width of the letter M
a brace is a support or stay

explanation.surface: Someone tries to find room at a newspaper office to live, though it is a tight fit.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street is the London street long home to Britain's newspapers, so its space is a printer's EM; 'though it's a' is linking.
explanation.definitionFit: A hug or embrace is an affectionate squeeze in someone's arms.

clue.text: Small drop not up to expectations

parts.note: short means small
a fall is a drop

explanation.surface: A slight dip leaves results below what was hoped.
explanation.definitionFit: A deficit, the amount by which something falls below what was required, is a failure to meet a target.

clue.text: Roam the mountains

explanation.surface: An invitation to wander across the hills.
explanation.definitionFit: To range is to wander freely; a range is also a chain of peaks.

clue.text: In summer going to the mountains first

parts.note: taken as written
August is a summer month, abbreviated AUG
the Urals are the mountain range between Europe and Asia; URAL stands for the range

explanation.surface: Someone sets off for a summer holiday in the mountains for the very first time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summer' is a month here, AUG for August; 'going to' just strings the pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: An opening or debut event, such as a maiden speech, is described as the first of its kind.

clue.text: Decor for a study?

parts.note: a pensive daydream is called a study of a certain colour, so the decorating scheme of that kind of study would be that colour

explanation.surface: A question about how to decorate a home office.
explanation.walkthrough: A BROWN study is an idiom for a state of absent-minded thought; the clue pretends the study is a room to paint.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'brown study' means deep reverie, so the colour scheme of such a study would be that dull earthy shade.

clue.text: Chess expert demonstrates the game for children

definitions.text: Chess expert demonstrates the game for children

parts.words: Chess expert demonstrates the game for children
parts.note: in chess the most important piece can make the special move of castling, so a chess player could be said to show that piece doing so; the same phrase names a playground game of claiming a mound

explanation.surface: A chess grandmaster shows a group of youngsters how to play.
explanation.walkthrough: The children's game is one where a player stands on a heap and fends off rivals; in chess the king can 'castle', so the phrase is read as a chess move.
explanation.definitionFit: The playground game has one child holding a mound or high point while the others try to push them off it.

clue.text: Design in an effort to be fashionable

indicators.note: the word for design is placed inside the word for an effort

parts.note: a try is an attempt or effort
an end is an aim or design, as in 'to that end'

explanation.surface: Someone works hard at a design in the hope of looking stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Design' is not a pattern but an intention, END, as in 'to this end'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something up to date with current styles is described as in vogue, following the latest trend.

clue.text: Two chaps from another age?

parts.note: Edward is a man's name
Ian is another man's name

explanation.surface: A pair of men seem to belong to a bygone era.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: the era is the reign of Edward VII, 1901–10.
explanation.definitionFit: The period of King Edward VII's reign in the early 1900s is a past era, so this adjective means belonging to it.

clue.text: Polite rationale absorbs men of :letters

indicators.note: the phrase polite rationale takes in, or holds within it, the letters of the answer

explanation.surface: A courteous line of reasoning wins over the academics.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the two words: poLITE RATIonale.
explanation.definitionFit: The educated, literary class of a society are its well-read intellectuals, scholars and writers.

clue.text: Side Tommy concealed audacity

indicators.note: the letters are disguised, their true form concealed by being rearranged

explanation.surface: A team's soldier keeps his cheek hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concealed' is an unusual anagram signal: the letters of SIDE TOMMY are disguised by shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Shameless boldness and lack of modesty is brazen nerve or effrontery.

clue.text: Artistic representations cut out in G and S

parts.note: to etch is to cut out a design into a metal plate
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Pictures cut out in Gilbert and Sullivan style.
explanation.walkthrough: G and S looks like Gilbert and Sullivan, the Victorian comic opera team; here the letters are taken as they stand.
explanation.definitionFit: Prints made from engraved metal plates are artworks depicting scenes.

clue.text: What oarsmen do to American craft

explanation.surface: A description of rowers handling small American vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it is what oarsmen do to boats; as one word it is the American term for small oared craft.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowers row their boats; in the US a small vessel propelled by oars is called by this compound name, Britain's rowing boat.

clue.text: Mouth opening - .force one to take one with difficulty

indicators.note: the letters are forced together awkwardly into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
I again stands for one

explanation.surface: An opening has to be forced to let something in, which proves hard.
explanation.walkthrough: FORCE plus two I's (one ... one) is rearranged; 'opening' sits between definition and fodder, part of the misleading picture.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperture of the body, such as the oral one, is a hole or opening.

clue.text: Device — imitation 'stone in Ireland's case

annotationWithheld.why: Device — imitation stone in Ireland's case (6), answer EMBLEM: 'Device' defines it, but no reading of 'imitation stone in Ireland's case' found builds EMBLEM; scan matches the held text and searches gave no parse

clue.text: You may have to use your bonce in most of this game

definitions.text: You may have to use your bonce in most of this game

parts.words: You may have to use your bonce in most of this game
parts.note: bonce is slang for the head, but it is also the name for a large playing piece in the children's game of rolling small glass balls

explanation.surface: A game that calls for you to use your head much of the time.
explanation.walkthrough: Bonce is British slang for head, and also a large marble; losing one's marbles means losing one's wits.
explanation.definitionFit: The children's game is played by flicking small glass balls, and the largest of them is called a bonce.

clue.text: National dog shows?

explanation.surface: A pedigree hound on display at a show.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is a native of Afghanistan; the second is the long-haired hound; 'shows?' is linking.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Afghanistan is a national of that country, and the elegant long-coated hound bred there takes its name.

clue.text: Making a beeline for an honest footballer?

explanation.surface: A direct run for goal by a player who never cheats.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer: an honest player is straight, and an attacking footballer is a forward.
explanation.definitionFit: Heading directly somewhere is going in a direct line; a direct, honest person is candid, and a straight forward is the jokey footballer.

clue.text: Hit that breaks records

explanation.surface: A chart-topping single that outsells all others.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge success is a hit record; and the word also means to shatter, as in breaking discs into pieces.

clue.text: Crime — sheet missing from Haworth residence

indicators.note: the word for sheet is taken away from the word for the residence

parts.note: the Brontë sisters lived at the parsonage in Haworth, a Yorkshire village
a page is a sheet of paper

explanation.surface: A sheet of paper has gone from the Brontës' Yorkshire home, which is a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: Haworth is the Yorkshire village where the Brontë family lived at the parsonage; P and AGE come out, leaving the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberately setting fire to property is a criminal offence.

clue.text: Baba a bit short in defensive argument

parts.note: the hero of the folk tale is Ali Baba, so the name that goes with Baba is Ali

indicators.note: the word is cut short by losing its last letter

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: A request to make something slightly shorter in a defence case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baba' gives ALI, the first half of the name Ali Baba; 'short' trims the T from BIT; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An accused person's defence that they were somewhere else when the crime happened is the classic plea of being elsewhere.

clue.text: Presumably nothing will satisfy them

parts.note: people who believe in nothing at all would be contented only by nothing, a play on the phrase about the hard to please

explanation.surface: A grumble about people who are impossible to please.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally, 'nothing' is what these believers hold to; Latin nihil means nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Philosophers who reject all values and beliefs are named from the Latin for nothing, so nothing is literally their creed.

clue.text: Food taken back out of rage from parasites

indicators.note: the reversed food word sits outside the word for rage, which comes out of its middle
the word for food is returned, read from its end to its start

parts.note: nosh is slang for food
rage is anger

explanation.surface: Someone loses their temper and snatches food back from spongers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken back' turns NOSH into HSON; 'out of' puts that outside ANGER, giving H-ANGER-SON.
explanation.definitionFit: Sycophantic followers who live off someone's success are spongers feeding on their host.

clue.text: Bonny by the Clyde

parts.note: the Clyde is the river of Glasgow, so the clue asks for the Scots word for bonny, healthy and attractive

explanation.surface: A Scottish word for good-looking.
explanation.walkthrough: The Clyde is the river through Glasgow, so 'by the Clyde' marks a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots dialect a buxom, comely, healthy-looking person is described with this word meaning pleasant-looking.
